item.title: Holocene and last interglacial relative sea level changes in Sri Lanka based on geological indicators
item.dc:creator: Amila Sandaruwan Ratnayake
item.description:
Discover Geoscience — matched: interglacial, last interglacial, Holocene, sea level, relative sea level
Earth’s climate oscillations between interglacial and glacial periods have driven significant sea level changes. Sri Lanka, located in the Indian Ocean, provides an ideal natural setting for studying paleo sea level changes. This study compiles 92 Holocene sea level records and identifies last interglacial stratigraphic evidence from Point Kudrimalai to reconstruct paleo sea level fluctuations in Sri Lanka. In addition, this study evaluates underutilized sea level indicators such as beachrock, coastal barrier sands, and mangrove swamps to address methodological challenges in reconstructing past sea levels. Results show that diverse sea level indicators, including beachrock, coastal barrier sands, raised marine deposits, and marine shell beds, primarily reflect Holocene sea level changes and their geological impacts. Using standardized sea level indicators such as coral and marine shell beds, this study reveals Holocene sea levels approximately 1.0–2.0 m above present between 6000 and 2000 cal BP. The 6–9 m elevation associated with Point Kudrimalai can possibly be correlated with regional Pleistocene sea level highstands. In contrast, the Palk Strait land bridge can be identified as a potential paleogeographic connection during periods of substantially lower sea level. Accordingly, these findings elucidate that the impact of sea level changes in Sri Lanka has likely influenced coastal geomorphology. Therefore, this reconstruction enhances understanding of regional sea level variability and its role in shaping coastal landscapes in the Indian Ocean.

item.title: Diverging runoff drives uncertainty in Antarctic surface mass balance projections under a high emission scenario
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Heurgue, Charles Amory, Christoph Kittel, Fredrik Boberg, Gaël Durand, Vincent Favier, … (+10)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, ice shelf, Antarctic, surface mass balance, sea level, emission scenario
We studied how the Antarctic ice sheet surface mass balance may change by 2100 using three high-resolution climate models forced by the same future climate scenario. While the models agree for present-day conditions, they project very different futures, especially over floating ice shelves. These differences mainly come from how melting, refreezing, and temperature are represented. Our results show that future sea level projections strongly depend on how well models simulate today’s climate.

item.title: Fusing a foundation model with spatiotemporal correction for automated long-term tracking of rift propagation from satellite imagery: a case study of the amery ice shelf
item.dc:creator: Zixiao Guo, Ronggang Huang, Yunfei Zhang, Yikai Zhu, Ruijie Chang, Qiang Shen, … (+2)
item.description:
GIScience & Remote Sensing — matched: ice shelf, Antarctic, sea level, sea-level rise
Long-term satellite monitoring of rift propagation is essential for assessing Antarctic ice shelf stability and projecting sea-level rise. Currently, long-term tracking of rifts still relies on time-consuming manual interpretation, significantly affecting its feasibility for large-scale rift monitoring. Here, we present a novel framework for automatically tracking rift propagation, which fuses the fine-tuned visual foundation model (Segment Anything Model, SAM) and spatiotemporal correction. The SAM enables automated rift extraction using only a few samples without any manual prompts, while the spatiotemporal correction improves the precision of rift mapping for geometric measurements. We applied this framework to automatically monitor key rifts on the Amery Ice Shelf using 768 Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 images from 2015 to 2025, achieving an F1 score of 98.6% across 11 independent scenes. Rift length and width measurements were in agreement with manual interpretation, with R2 values of 0.979 and 0.999, respectively. Furthermore, our extended monitoring revealed recent structural changes within the rift system on the Amery Ice Shelf. This study offers a new way for automated rift tracking with the foundation model for the first time, having significant potential for long-term monitoring of pan-Antarctic rifts.

item.title: TitanMPAS - a new global and regional Titan atmospheric circulation model. Part I: Global model results
item.dc:creator: Yuan Lian, Mark I. Richardson, Claire E. Newman, Martin A. Cordiner
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: insolation, regional climate model, reanalysis, parameterization
arXiv:2611.08700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We developed TitanMPAS, a new Titan global and regional climate model, to simulate atmospheric dynamics and methane cycles. It integrates the non-hydrostatic MPAS dynamical core and TitanWRF physics parameterizations, with corrections to relax the thin-atmosphere assumptions on the gravity and curvature terms. TitanMPAS improves upon TitanWRF by incorporating a better moist convection parameterization and the observed surface properties. Long-term simulations ($>$100 Titan years) with a high resolution of $1^\circ$ and the realistic topography show that TitanMPAS is able to produce the stratospheric superrotation with typical equatorial wind speed over $\rm 120\,ms^{-1}$ and the maximum zonal wind speed exceeding $\rm 170\,ms^{-1}$ . Besides the good match of temperature profiles to the Cassini CIRS observations, the simulated wind, temperature and methane abundance in the troposphere match well with Huygens probe in-situ measurements. TitanMPAS also captures the major features of seasonal methane precipitation distribution patterns inferred from the observed cloud activities, as well as the vertical and latitudinal variations of methane abundance in the reanalysis of Cassini VIMS data. Resolution sensitivity studies show that higher resolution produces faster stratospheric superrotation, as well as stronger near-surface wind due to better resolved terrain variations. We further demonstrate that, despite the weak solar insolation, the near-surface temperature, pressure, wind magnitude and methane abundance all exhibit diurnal variations. Lastly, we show potential impacts of topography on methane transport and eddy momentum flux in both troposphere and stratosphere, which should be investigated in a future study.

item.title: Remote sensing of lake surface water temperature reveals divergent hydroclimatic associations with lake ice phenology across China
item.dc:creator: Qian Yang, Junyi Chang, Wendi Luo, Hongjun Su, Jintao Li, Nan Lin, … (+7)
item.category: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
item.description:
International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation — matched: machine learning, remote sensing, climate change
Lake ice phenology is a sensitive indicator of climate change, yet its regional hydroclimatic associations remain poorly understood. Here, we reconstructed daily lake surface water temperature (LSWT) from MODIS for 583 lakes across China and derived freeze-up date (FUD), break-up date (BUD), and ice cover duration (ICD) for 376 seasonally ice-covered lakes. Robustness was evaluated with sensitivity tests, meteorological observations, transition-period comparisons, and passive-microwave ice records; Mann-Kendall tests, Theil-Sen slopes, VIF-constrained XGBoost-SHAP, and structural equation modeling assessed trends and regional associations. FUD was delayed in all three ice-covered regions, whereas BUD was delayed in the Tibetan Plateau Lake Region (TPR) but advanced in the Mongolian-Xinjiang Lake Region (MXR) and Northeast Lake Region (NLR), resulting in shorter ICD in all regions. Regional mean ICD declined by 0.03, 0.35, and 0.47 d yr -1 in the TPR, MXR, and NLR, respectively; significant lake-level changes were concentrated in the TPR, with 72 and 33 lakes showing significant FUD and BUD trends. All nine models retained positive hold-out R 2 (0.535–0.960). SHAP attributions differed by region: radiative variables dominated in the TPR, the MXR showed metric-specific associations with wind, snowfall, geographic, and thermal , and geographic, radiative, and morphometric variables dominated in the NLR. Structural equation models indicated stronger precipitation-related associations in the NLR and snowfall-related associations in the MXR and TPR. These results reveal pronounced regional heterogeneity in lake ice responses to warming and the value of integrating remote sensing, interpretable machine learning, and pathway modeling to resolve these contrasts.

item.title: Climate change induced hydrological regime shifts in the transboundary Zarafshon River Basin in Central Asia
item.dc:creator: Sonu Khanal, Philip Kraaijenbrink, Faezeh Maghami Nick, Joel Fiddes, Arthur Lutz, Evan Miles, … (+4)
item.description:
Journal of Hydrology — matched: glacier, climate change, SSP
Mountain river basins in Central Asia are highly sensitive to climate-driven changes in snow and glacier melt, yet the magnitude and timing of the resulting hydrological regime shifts remain poorly quantified. To address this gap, we assess present and future hydrological shifts in the transboundary Zarafshon River Basin with the SPHY glacio-hydrological model. We improved the representation of snowmelt and snow infiltration, which redistributes water to delayed baseflow and improves winter and spring discharge. We calibrated the improved model against discharge observations, satellite-derived snow cover and glacier mass balance data through Monte Carlo optimization. Over 1991–2020, snowmelt dominates runoff (52.4%), followed by baseflow (23.3%) and rainfall-runoff (21.1%), whereas glacier melt contributes 3.2% but sustains late-summer low flows. Snow and glacier melt dominate the upstream hydrology, whereas rainfall-runoff and baseflow sustain the flow in the lower basin. Using downscaled ISIMIP3b climate scenarios, we project glacier volume to decline by ∼ 40% under SSP126 and ∼ 80% under SSP585 by 2100. Annual total runoff declines by less than 7% in all scenarios, because gains in rainfall-runoff and baseflow almost offset the melt loss. Peak total runoff declines by 22.6% under SSP585, and the annual peak discharge shifts earlier by 22–38 days. The hydrological regime shift from snowmelt to rainfall-runoff is more pronounced in the Fondarya than in the Matcha River system. These results indicate a shift from a snowmelt to a rainfall-runoff dominated hydrological regime. Such a shift would reduce summer water availability and increase irrigation stress, highlighting the need for adaptive management.

item.title: First discovery of the Kobayashi-Kasamori (Kb-Ks) tephra layer in terrestrial sediments of the Korean Peninsula
item.dc:creator: Seungwon Shin, Jin‐Young Lee, Seok‐Hwi Hong, Wook‐Hyun Nahm, Hyoun Soo Lim, Hyoun Soo Lim
item.description:
Quaternary Science Reviews — matched: paleoclimate, Quaternary
Abstract It was recently reported that a Quaternary basin in southeastern Korea was formed by a meteorite impact, and a 12-cm-thick tephra layer was found in lake sediments in this basin. In this study, we analyzed the geochemical composition and refractive index of glass shards to identify the unknown tephra. Based on both results, this tephra was identified as Kb-Ks tephra that erupted in the Kyushu area, Japan, approximately 520 ka. To our knowledge, this is the first report of Kb-Ks tephra in terrestrial sediments in the Korean Peninsula. These findings indicate that the depositional age of the lake sediments is much older than previously suspected (ca. 63 ka), and that the meteorite impact occurred before 520 ka. Although more detailed studies are needed, the discovery of Kb-Ks tephra provides important information concerning the paleoclimate during the middle Pleistocene, as well as the prediction of volcanic hazards in the Korean Peninsula.

item.title: Conservation of heat in the Coupled Arctic Prediction System (CAPS v1.1): comprehensive model evaluation based on the MOSAiC observations
item.dc:creator: Chao-Yuan Yang, Fengguan Gu, Jiping Liu, Annette Rinke, Hu Yang, Xiaoxu Shi
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: Arctic, sea ice
Accurately exchanging energy between the atmosphere and the ocean-ice systems through surface heat fluxes is crucial for climate modelling. We present an improved version of Coupled Arctic Prediction System (CAPS) by revising flux coupling for conservation of heat. Our results show that the model with improved flux coupling can better simulate sea ice conditions during the period of Multidisciplinary drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC).

item.title: Sensitivity of the IceCube atmospheric muon rate to decadal trends in the effective atmospheric temperature
item.dc:creator: Tanvi Krishnan, Gabriela Barenboim, Carlos A. Arg\"uelles
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: Antarctic, polar, reanalysis
arXiv:2611.00918v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decadal changes in the Antarctic stratosphere, generally associated with ozone recovery and shifts in polar circulation, are of broad geophysical interest. However, independent long-term measurements of the atmosphere above the Antarctic interior are scarce. We assess whether the atmospheric muon rate recorded by IceCube could constrain decadal changes in the effective atmospheric temperature, $T_\mathrm{eff}$, a weighted average of temperature through the atmosphere that is most sensitive to the stratosphere. Using public atmospheric reanalysis data and records of cosmic-ray, solar, and geomagnetic variability, we reproduce the measured seasonal response of the IceCube muon rate. We then test whether the same response applies to long-term temperature changes with a different vertical temperature profile. The limiting requirement is detector stability rather than counting statistics: an unmodeled muon rate drift of $1\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$ would mimic a temperature trend of $2.8\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. The long-term rate must therefore be stable to approximately $0.3\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$. Within this budget, snow accumulation contributions can be constrained. For a 14-year record, atmospheric variability gives a one-sided 95% CL statistical sensitivity of $1.6\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. Given this sensitivity, the $\sim0.9,\mathrm{K,decade^{-1}}$ cooling indicated by the 2011-2025 atmospheric records would be constrained at the 95% confidence level after approximately 22 years of measurement.

item.title: Temporal variability of mineral dust composition on an alpine snowpack in the Tateyama Mountains, Japan
item.dc:creator: Pia Ataka, Ryo Sugiyama, Noboru Furukawa, Nozomu Takeuchi
item.description:
Polar Science — matched: glacier, snowpack
Mineral dust is one of the major light-absorbing impurities in snow and ice, and affects snowpack and glacier melting. However, the origin and composition of mineral dust deposited on snow surfaces, and how these vary over time and space, remain poorly understood. This study examined the temporal and spatial variability in the composition of mineral dust in an alpine snowpack in the Tateyama Mountains, Japan and evaluated the relative contributions of long-range-transported and locally derived dust to dust deposition on the snow surface. Surface snow samples collected from April to July were analyzed using microscopy, SEM–EDS, and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The results showed a clear temporal transition in the mineral assemblages. The April samples were dominated by quartz and feldspar, consistent with long-range-transported Asian dust. Conversely, samples from May to July showed increasing abundances of chlorite, biotite, and amphibole, indicating a growing contribution of locally derived dust during the melt season. Coarse, feldspar-rich dust was frequently observed near diorite outcrops. These results indicate that Asian dust dominated in spring, whereas locally derived dust increasingly contributed to the mineral composition of surface snow during the melt season. This suggests that local geology plays an important role in controlling snowpack impurity composition, with potential implications for snow-surface radiative properties.

item.title: Reconciling advective upwelling with diapycnal downwelling: A transient kinematic perspective on Munk's conundrum
item.dc:creator: Lei Han
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: Antarctic
arXiv:2502.21006v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bottom-intensified turbulent fluxes observed near the seafloor drive abyssal densification and diapycnal downwelling through their vertical divergence. This appears paradoxical under steady stratification because dense bottom waters continuously enter from Antarctic sources. Motivated by evolving Indo-Pacific stratification, we use idealized simulations to examine abyssal overturning under transient and steady-state conditions. Using a kinematic rather than thermodynamic water-mass-transformation approach, we diagnose advective overturning, isopycnal volume tendency, and diapycnal transport in two cooling experiments with different mixing intensities, one warming experiment, and one quasi-equilibrium experiment. Advective upwelling occurs in all four, whereas diagnosed diapycnal transport varies in direction. In Type-I cooling, the isopycnal volume tendency exceeds advective overturning in magnitude, yielding downward diapycnal transport; in Type-II cooling, advective overturning exceeds the isopycnal volume tendency, yielding upward diapycnal transport. The warming and quasi-equilibrium experiments also exhibit upward diapycnal transport. These relationships persist qualitatively in potential-temperature coordinates. Type-I cooling also spontaneously produces an observationally documented bottom-intensified buoyancy-flux profile with an e-folding scale comparable to previous estimates. Thus, cooling alone does not determine diapycnal transport direction; it depends kinematically on the relative strengths of advective overturning and isopycnal volume tendency. Within this idealized framework, the results provide a transient kinematic interpretation of the interior-downwelling conundrum: abyssal waters can rise through the basin interior while undergoing diapycnal downwelling, without requiring an upslope return pathway within the bottom boundary layer.

item.title: Evaluation and improvement of CAMS-derived CCN number concentrations using in-situ measurements
item.dc:creator: Yannick Emanuel Anders, Karoline Block, Mira Pöhlker, Johannes Quaas
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Particles in the atmosphere can trigger the formation of cloud droplets, affecting cloud properties and climate. This study evaluates a new global dataset of these particles with measurements from 25 sites around the world. The variability in time and space and their conditional formation behaviour is analysed. The authors identify systematic biases and introduce a simple correction based on observations that greatly improves the dataset's accuracy.
